core: Working definition of health promotion, attributed to WHO and first set out in the Ottawa Charter of 1986: the process of enabling people to increase control over, and to improve, their health
The one-sentence line between promotion and prevention: promotion enables health, prevention stops disease (the deep prevention story is owned by the sibling prevention topic)
The four levels of health promotion, individual, community, policy, and environment, each with one line and an original example

The Ottawa Charter prerequisites for health: peace, shelter, education, food, income, a stable eco-system, sustainable resources, social justice, and equity, presented as the foundation health is built on
Health promotion in practice: campaigns, healthy settings, and supportive policies, each with one line
The honest reality check: promotion works best when the environment supports the healthy choice, making the healthy choice the easy choice
supporting: The Charter's three strategies, advocate, enable, and mediate, anchoring how promotion acts at each level
WHO's settings approach with the Healthy Cities programme as its best-known example, and the healthy-settings principles of community participation, partnership, empowerment, and equity
WHO's governance-and-policies framing that healthy choices should be accessible and affordable to all

Healthy People 2030's statement that the conditions in the settings where people are born, live, learn, work, play, worship, and age affect health outcomes and risks, corroborating the environment-first note

claims.claim: The Ottawa Charter for Health Promotion, adopted at WHO's First International Conference on Health Promotion in Ottawa in 1986, defines health promotion as the process of enabling people to increase control over, and to improve, their health, a working definition WHO still uses.

The Ottawa Charter names peace, shelter, education, food, income, a stable eco-system, sustainable resources, social justice, and equity as the fundamental conditions and resources for health, i.e. the prerequisites for health.

The Ottawa Charter sets out three strategies for health promotion: advocate, to push for conditions that favor health; enable, to give people the skills and opportunities to take control of their health; and mediate, to coordinate action across governments, sectors, and communities.

The Ottawa Charter states that people cannot achieve their fullest health potential unless they are able to take control of the things that determine their health, and that this control requires a secure foundation in a supportive environment.

WHO describes health promotion as operating through healthy public policy, supportive environments, and community action, and names the settings approach, rooted in the Charter, with principles of community participation, partnership, empowerment, and equity, with the Healthy Cities programme as its best-known example.
WHO promotes strengthening governance and policies so that healthy choices are accessible and affordable to all, the supportive-policies shape of health promotion in practice.

The U.S. Healthy People 2030 framework states that the conditions in the settings where people are born, live, learn, work, play, worship, and age affect health outcomes and risks, supporting the environment-first note on why promotion succeeds or falls short.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Where health promotion ends and disease prevention begins is drawn differently across WHO documents and popular materials.
positions: WHO's Health Promotion Glossary treats disease prevention as measures that reduce risk factors and disease occurrence, distinct from health promotion as enabling people to increase control over their health.
Popular materials often blur the two, calling any health-related campaign promotion and any clinical measure prevention.
The two overlap in practice, e.g. a salt-cutting cooking class can be framed either way.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson keeps the line the Charter draws: promotion enables health, prevention stops disease, and the deep prevention story is owned by the sibling prevention topic, which this lesson references without teaching.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The phrase 'make the healthy choice the easy choice' is widely quoted in health promotion but is an informal slogan, not a formal WHO definition.
positions: Some materials attribute the phrase to WHO or to the Ottawa Charter tradition.
Others treat promotion as purely about environmental change, ignoring the individual and community levels.
The Charter itself speaks of a supportive environment and prerequisites rather than this slogan.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the phrase as a slogan that captures the field's temperament, not a law, and anchors it to the Charter's supportive-environment principle while keeping all four levels in view.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The prerequisites-for-health list varies in length and wording across WHO documents over time.
positions: The 1986 Charter lists peace, shelter, education, food, income, a stable eco-system, sustainable resources, social justice, and equity.
Later WHO documents compress or reorder the list, and some add items such as empowerment and social support.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the Charter's own 1986 list, dated and attributed to 1986, and does not present it as an exhaustive modern inventory.

rightsIssues: The Ottawa Charter publication page is WHO-copyrighted; the Charter's definition and prerequisites are paraphrased in original prose with short attributed quotations, not reproduced verbatim at length.
WHO health-topic pages are public-facing but copyrighted; facts are synthesized in original wording with attribution, and no page prose is reproduced.
The Healthy People 2030 page is a U.S. government work (public domain), attributed.

sourceRecords.title: Ottawa Charter for Health Promotion, 1986
sourceRecords.license: WHO copyright; Charter text paraphrased with short attributed quotations, facts restated in original prose
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). The publication page reproduces the Ottawa Charter for Health Promotion adopted at the First International Conference on Health Promotion, Ottawa, Canada, 17-21 November 1986. Supports: the working definition of health promotion as the process of enabling people to increase control over, and to improve, their health; health as a resource for everyday life, not the objective of living; the three strategies of advocate, enable, and mediate; the prerequisites list (peace, shelter, education, food, income, a stable eco-system, sustainable resources, social justice, and equity); and the statement that people cannot achieve their fullest health potential unless they take control of the things that determine their health, which requires a secure foundation in a supportive environment. All restated in original prose with short attributed quotations.

sourceRecords.license: WHO public-facing page; facts synthesized in original wording, no prose reproduced
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: the WHO framing of health promotion as the process of enabling people to increase control over, and to improve, their health (the definition carried from the Ottawa Charter and the Health Promotion Glossary); health promotion as more than health care, operating through healthy public policy, supportive environments, and community action; the settings approach rooted in the Charter, with principles of community participation, partnership, empowerment, and equity, and the Healthy Cities programme as its best-known example; and strengthening governance and policies to make healthy choices accessible and affordable to all. Facts synthesized in original wording; no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Social Determinants of Health — Healthy People 2030
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), Office of Disease Prevention and Health Promotion
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Page carries an HHS restoration banner (court order) but the SDOH framework content was intact when read: SDOH definition (conditions in the environments where people are born, live, learn, work, play, worship, and age); the five domains (economic stability, education access and quality, health care access and quality, neighborhood and built environment, social and community context); examples including safe housing, transportation, neighborhoods, access to nutritious foods, and the grocery-store nutrition example; SDOH contributing to wide health disparities and inequities; the upstream-factors framing. Cited here for the environment-shapes-health statement behind the lesson's honest note that a campaign lands or falls on the environment.
